items.title: Langfuse dataset reruns blending old and new scores into one review surface
items.why_now: A fresh Langfuse issue shows dataset evaluations rerun under the same name can display the newest traces while run-level scores still aggregate older executions underneath. Review systems become misleading when visible examples and aggregate judgments are computed over different behavioral histories.
items.format: LinkedIn post, short thread, or builder reply
questions: What is the best plain-English way to explain why rerun semantics matter more than another dashboard widget?
Is the sharper framing here about hidden regressions, review-loop trust, or dataset version boundaries?

items.title: The real product skill is getting from "something feels off" to the underlying rows
items.why_now: Repeated in Drive assets and the 60-day roadmap. Teams need a repeatable path from a vague complaint to the underlying rows.
items.format: LinkedIn post, short thread, or podcast talking point
questions: What is the plainest way to describe the move from vague complaint to inspectable evidence without sounding like generic observability?
Do you want to anchor this in one concrete example or keep it at the workflow level?

items.title: Session review matters because many failures look like recovery until you inspect the whole conversation
items.why_now: New asset PDF calls out identifying sessions where users stop making progress. HF dataset-viewer adding session_id support for Claude traces corroborates it.
items.format: LinkedIn post, short thread, or interview prompt
questions: What are the best concrete signs that a session has stopped making progress even though the model is still producing text?
Is the sharper framing "stuck sessions" or "false recovery"?

items.title: Weekly review ownership is the real habit behind improving AI products over time
items.why_now: Three internal docs all push the same idea: someone should review real production behavior weekly instead of waiting for a bug report.
items.format: LinkedIn post or short X thread
questions: Do you want this framed as a founder lesson, a team-process lesson, or a product-design lesson?
